text:
Sampled-negative HR@10 measures a different ranking task from full-catalog HR@10; model orderings can reverse even in expectation. [Krichene and Rendle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02263) establish this inconsistency; a [RecSys 2025 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05398) examines sampling fidelity, separability, robustness to exposure bias, and alignment with ground-truth preferences. For this benchmark, retain the pinned 99-negative evaluator and four-category macro HR@10 as the selection objective. Label full-catalog results separately; neither protocol establishes unobserved user preferences.

Recommended diagnostic design: record each validation target’s rank, rank histogram, HR@10, and fraction of candidates outranking it. These statistics are invariant to strictly increasing score transformations; raw training-pair margins are not. Use the evaluator’s tie handling. Across checkpoints, measure whether diagnostic changes track per-category and macro HR@10 changes; correlations from adaptively selected checkpoints remain exploratory. Report popularity and history-length slices using training interactions only, with slice counts and uncertainty. Keep full-catalog recommendation coverage and popularity concentration separate from accuracy claims.

For comparisons, resample users with replacement within each category, retaining paired baseline/candidate outcomes and fixed candidate sets; recompute the equal-weight four-category mean difference for every bootstrap replicate. Report the difference and 95% interval. [Paired bootstrap methodology](https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/P18-1128.pdf) supports matched comparisons, but these intervals condition on the sampled candidates and trained models. They do not account for training-seed variability or adaptive winner selection. [Holdout-reuse research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629) explains why repeated feedback can overfit validation: log all trials, limit adaptive queries, and treat winner intervals as descriptive without changing splits or accessing hidden tests.
